questions.text: In the pure death process with N0=100 cells and individual death rate μ=0.2/day, what is P(a specific cell is still alive at t=3 days)?
questions.explanation: Each cell's lifetime is Exp(μ) = Exp(0.2). P(survive to t=3) = P(T>3) = e^{-μt} = e^{-0.2×3} = e^{-0.6} ≈ 0.549. This is the individual survival probability p(t), the parameter of the Binomial distribution for the full population.

questions.text: In the pure death process starting with N0 individuals, N(t) follows a Binomial(N0, e^{-μt}) distribution.
questions.explanation: Each of the N0 individuals survives to time t independently with probability p(t) = e^{-μt}. The number surviving is therefore the count of 'successes' in N0 independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p(t) — exactly Binomial(N0, e^{-μt}).

questions.text: In the pure death process ODE: dP_n/dt = -(nμ)P_n + (n+1)μ P_{n+1}. The term (n+1)μ P_{n+1} represents:
options: The rate of leaving state n (one cell dies, population goes from n to n-1)
The rate of entering state n from state n+1 (one death decreases population by 1)
The birth rate compensating for deaths
The probability that exactly n+1 cells die
questions.explanation: The term +(n+1)μ P_{n+1} is a 'source' term: the process is in state n+1, and one death occurs (at rate (n+1)μ when n+1 cells are present), bringing the population to n. This is a 'flow in' to state n from state n+1.

questions.text: With N0=1000 cancer cells and μ=0.5/day, what is the expected number surviving after 10 days?
questions.explanation: E[N(t)] = N0 × e^{-μt} = 1000 × e^{-0.5×10} = 1000 × e^{-5} ≈ 1000 × 0.00674 ≈ 6.74 cells. After 10 days of chemotherapy at rate 0.5/day, only about 7 cells are expected to survive.

questions.text: The expected extinction time in the pure death process starting with N0 individuals is (1/μ)×H_{N0}, where H_{N0} is the N0-th harmonic number. For N0=10 and μ=1, H_{10} ≈ 2.93. What is E[T_ext]?
questions.explanation: E[T_ext] = (1/μ) × H_{N0} = (1/1) × 2.93 = 2.93 time units. This is much longer than the individual expected lifetime 1/μ = 1, because the last survivor must outlive all other N0-1 individuals.

questions.text: The variance of N(t) in the pure death process is maximised at t = ln(2)/μ (when exactly half the population has died on average).
questions.explanation: Var[N(t)] = N0 × p(t) × (1-p(t)) where p(t)=e^{-μt}. For a Binomial, variance np(1-p) is maximised at p=1/2, which occurs when e^{-μt}=1/2, i.e., t=ln(2)/μ. At this point, the population is most uncertain — some simulations will have many survivors, others few.
